title: The LLM stopped calling. The tool never did.
summary: Model-call limits protect the outer agent loop. They do not stop code that is already running forever inside a sandbox.
symptoms: One tool invocation stays in-flight while the LLM-call counter stops moving.
Sandbox CPU, memory, process count or output keeps growing.
User cancellation returns, but the tool process or its children keep running.
failure_boundary: The hand-off from orchestrator → executable process. Once code is running, model-step limits no longer own termination.
why: Agent runtimes usually cap model turns, tokens or tool calls. Those controls help when the model repeatedly asks for more work. A single tool call is different: generated code can deadlock, recurse, block on I/O, spawn children, flood stdout or loop forever without making another LLM request.
example: A code tool runs generated Python containing a retry loop with no terminal condition. The agent has a 20-call budget, but it used only one call. The sandbox burns a CPU core for an hour because the component that owns the LLM budget is not the component that owns the process.
fooled: cancelling the model request but not the process tree
prevent: Run executable code in a separate process/container with an external supervisor.
Enforce per-invocation wall-clock TTL plus overall task deadline.
Apply CPU, memory, PID/thread, file-descriptor, disk, output and network budgets at the sandbox boundary.
Prefer narrow typed tools when arbitrary code execution is not required.
detect: Emit heartbeat/progress events for long-running tools and alert on progress silence.
Track wall time and CPU time per invocation, not only model/tool-call counts.
Record code/tool hash and process-tree metadata so repeated hangs can be quarantined.
recover: TERM → bounded grace period → KILL the entire process group/container.
Destroy a hard-timed-out sandbox instead of returning it to the pool.
Return an explicit TOOL_TIMEOUT/TOOL_KILLED state; never disguise it as a normal tool response.
test: side effect commits, then tool hangs
invariant: Every tool invocation has an owner outside the tool that can terminate its full process tree within a bounded time.
closing: An agent-step limit controls the agent. A sandbox deadline controls the code. Production needs both.
first_five: Find the sandbox/container and current process tree.
Check wall-clock age, CPU time, RSS, output bytes and last progress heartbeat.
Terminate through the supervisor; if the tool can write externally, reconcile side effects before retry.
flow_caption: Outer loop: 1 call. Inner execution: unbounded.

title: One inference region failed. Traffic kept going there.
summary: Multi-region inventory is not resilience if the router cannot eject an unhealthy model endpoint.
symptoms: A fixed fraction of requests return 5xx/timeouts.
Other regions remain healthy and have spare capacity.
Removing one endpoint from the pool immediately improves success rate.
failure_boundary: The routing layer fails to translate per-region health into traffic decisions quickly enough.
why: Static round-robin spreads healthy traffic and unhealthy traffic equally. A resilient model gateway needs region-level health, bounded retries, endpoint ejection and enough headroom for the surviving regions.
example: A six-region inference pool loses one region after a provider-side change. Five regions are healthy, but roughly one-sixth of requests continue failing because the router keeps treating every endpoint as equal.
fooled: health checks that prove only DNS/TCP reachability
prevent: Use active inference probes plus rolling failure/latency health per region.
Reserve failover headroom and enforce per-region circuit breakers.
Classify retryable failures and cap the retry budget.
Version routing configuration and use controlled re-entry after recovery.
detect: Dashboard success, latency, throttling and saturation by endpoint.
Compare router decisions with endpoint-health state.
Probe independently of user traffic so a quiet region can still be declared unhealthy.
recover: Automatically eject after a bounded unhealthy threshold.
Shift only to regions with confirmed headroom.
Reintroduce with canary traffic, then ramp.
test: failover while survivors are near capacity
invariant: If healthy serving capacity still exists, loss of one region must not become loss of the product.
closing: Redundancy is inventory. Resilience is routing away from the broken copy.
first_five: Break errors down by region/deployment rather than global averages.
Eject the bad endpoint and verify remaining capacity before shifting traffic.
Watch retry amplification and queue growth after the shift.
flow_caption: Redundancy exists; failure isolation does not.

title: Config said the model existed. The provider said 404.
summary: Your model catalog can stay green after the actual serving deployment has been removed, renamed or retired.
symptoms: A deterministic model-not-found error repeats across retries.
Internal config/database still marks the deployment active.
Restarts do nothing because the bad reference is durable.
failure_boundary: Internal control-plane truth diverges from provider serving-plane truth.
why: Model IDs are copied into catalogs, agent records, feature flags and deployment manifests. Provider inventory changes independently. Without reconciliation, stale references can outlive the resource they point to.
example: A dedicated deployment is removed during migration, but active agents still reference its old deployment key. Every call fails deterministically; retries only generate more identical 404s.
fooled: validating only at agent creation time
deleting before proving zero live references
prevent: Run a reconciler between internal model catalog and provider inventory.
Block retirement while active references remain.
Preflight deployment existence during release and agent activation.
Use staged retirement: announce → migrate → drain → verify → remove.
detect: Alert separately on model/deployment-not-found.
Continuously report configured-vs-serving drift.
Track live consumers per model/deployment version.
recover: Stop retrying the missing target.
Route to a pre-validated compatible target when policy permits.
Repair config and verify all consumers converge.
invariant: Every enabled model reference resolves to a serving deployment that the runtime can actually call.
closing: A model name in a database is not a serving model.
first_five: Classify the error as deterministic, not transient.
Compare the referenced deployment ID with live provider inventory.
Stop retries, choose a validated target, then repair the durable reference.
flow_caption: Two control planes, two different realities.

title: The primary model hit capacity. The workflow had nowhere to go.
summary: Quota and concurrency limits are normal. An outage happens when the system has no bounded degraded mode.
symptoms: Failures rise only during traffic spikes.
Concurrency/token throughput reaches a provider or deployment limit.
Retries and backlog grow together.
failure_boundary: A bounded inference tier reaches capacity, but the runtime has only one admissible execution path.
why: Inference capacity is finite even when APIs feel elastic. Blind retries amplify pressure. A fallback model also changes behavior, so failover is safe only when the alternate path has workflow-specific eval coverage.
example: A morning burst exceeds the preferred model's concurrency allowance. Without admission control or a validated fallback, excess requests fail, retries multiply, and a queue grows faster than it can drain.
fooled: assuming a smaller model is behaviorally equivalent
prevent: Set explicit per-model concurrency/token budgets and priority classes.
Validate fallback models on workflow-specific golden/eval slices.
Bound queue size and queue age; propagate backpressure upstream.
Define degraded modes: lower-cost model, reduced scope, queued execution or human path.
detect: Track capacity utilization, throttle rate, queue age and retry volume.
Measure quality/tool-choice drift during fallback.
Separate overload from provider faults and application faults.
recover: Shed/defer low-priority work first.
Route eligible work to validated capacity.
Drain backlog gradually after recovery.
invariant: Capacity exhaustion produces a bounded, intentional degraded mode—not an uncontrolled retry cascade.
closing: Fallback is not a model name in config. It is a tested operating mode.
first_five: Confirm saturation vs application error using capacity telemetry.
Stop retry amplification and protect critical traffic with admission control.
Activate only a pre-tested fallback/degraded mode.
flow_caption: Overload must become a policy decision, not a retry storm.

title: The next message hit another worker—and the conversation disappeared.
summary: Session affinity can hide a state-design bug until autoscaling, failover or cross-zone routing moves the next turn.
symptoms: Follow-up questions look like brand-new conversations.
The bug is intermittent and worse after scaling or failover.
Single-node tests pass; multi-replica production fails.
failure_boundary: Correctness depends on process-local state that is not reconstructable on another healthy worker.
why: Sticky sessions improve locality, but they are not durable state. Workers restart and requests move. Conversation history, sequence/version and workflow control state need a shared source of truth when continuity matters.
example: Turn one lands on worker A and stores context only in memory. Turn two lands on worker B after a routing change. The request is valid, but the model lacks the prior state needed to interpret it.
prevent: Persist canonical conversation/workflow state outside the worker.
Use affinity only as a locality optimization.
Carry stable conversation ID plus monotonic sequence/version.
Use optimistic concurrency or equivalent protection against stale overwrites.
detect: Log worker/region, state source and version for every turn.
Alert on context misses, sequence gaps and unexpected session resets.
Trace cross-worker state reconstruction latency.
recover: Reload latest durable state on routing miss.
Reject or reconcile stale/out-of-order updates.
Rebuild transient caches from durable history.
invariant: Any healthy worker receiving a valid conversation ID can reconstruct the state needed to continue correctly.
closing: Affinity may improve locality. Correctness should not depend on one process staying alive.
first_five: Compare routing target across adjacent turns.
Inspect conversation version/sequence and where state was loaded from.
Force a durable reload and check for stale/out-of-order writes.
flow_caption: Routing moved; the state did not.

title: The credential rotated. The running agent did not.
summary: A valid security rotation can break long-lived agents that cache identity once and never refresh it.
symptoms: A healthy tool suddenly starts returning auth failures after rotation.
Restarting the worker fixes the problem.
New workers succeed while old workers fail.
failure_boundary: The secret/identity source has moved to version N+1 while a live process still holds version N.
why: Long-running agents can outlive passwords, tokens and client sessions. Updating the secret store does not mutate objects already loaded into a process. Rotation needs a convergence path for live consumers.
example: An overnight job authenticates at startup. Credentials rotate two hours later. New workers use the new version, but the existing worker keeps reusing a stale client and every API call begins failing.
fooled: restart as the normal rotation mechanism
prevent: Prefer short-lived workload identity/credentials when possible.
Use a version-aware secret provider, not static startup config.
Refresh before expiry and on classified authentication failure.
Support client/session recreation without restarting the workflow.
detect: Expose non-secret credential version/lease age.
Alert on consumers using a superseded version.
Correlate rotation event → auth error → successful refresh.
recover: Invalidate stale client state and fetch current identity.
Retry only after successful refresh within a bounded policy.
Checkpoint long-running work so re-auth does not restart from zero.
invariant: Authorized credential rotation must not require manual worker restarts or leave live agents using stale authority.
closing: Rotation is complete when live consumers converge, not when the vault changes.
first_five: Correlate auth failures with recent rotation events.
Compare credential-version metadata between failing and fresh workers without logging the secret.
Invalidate/recreate the client and verify re-auth before retrying work.
flow_caption: The vault changed. Process memory did not.

title: Two valid triggers started processing the same work.
summary: A webhook and a poller can each be correct and still create duplicate or conflicting execution together.
symptoms: Duplicate replies/actions appear for the same source event.
One consumer makes the item disappear before another sees it.
Disabling either path removes the bug.
failure_boundary: Ownership is implicit: two consumers independently believe they own the same external event.
why: Real-time triggers are often added before scheduled paths are fully retired. If both watch the same mailbox, queue or record transition, timing determines which workflow wins. Idempotency reduces damage, but ownership still needs to be explicit.
example: A poller processes unread requests every few minutes. Later a webhook is enabled for the same source. The webhook handles the item first and changes its state; the poller either misses it or performs a second side effect.
fooled: source state such as unread = ownership
prevent: Choose one authoritative ingestion path per event class—or coordinate ownership explicitly.
Use stable event IDs plus a durable inbox/dedupe record.
Use leases/fencing when only one worker may own the event.
Inventory webhook, poller and schedule lifecycle centrally.
detect: Alert on multiple claims for one event ID.
Trace trigger → claim → side effect end-to-end.
Continuously inventory active subscriptions and schedules.
recover: Disable/expire the unintended trigger.
Reconcile side effects before replay.
Backfill from source of truth through the dedupe path.
invariant: Every external event has one identifiable execution owner—or the system can prove multiple consumers are safe.
closing: Two correct pipelines can make one incorrect system when ownership is implicit.
first_five: Trace the same event ID across every ingestion path.
Disable the unintended owner before replaying anything.
Reconcile already-produced side effects, then backfill with dedupe enabled.
flow_caption: Two ingestion paths, one piece of work.

title: One RAG flag turned a small question into thousands of clauses.
summary: Hybrid retrieval can fail before retrieval begins when rewrites, filters and expansions multiply into an oversized search plan.
symptoms: Search fails on a query-complexity/clause limit.
Only specific tenants, filters or feature flags trigger it.
A simpler retrieval path immediately works.
failure_boundary: Complexity is created after the user question but before the search engine: query planning becomes the failure point.
why: Hybrid search may combine query rewrites, lexical terms, vector searches, metadata filters, entitlements and synonyms. Multiplicative expansion can cross hard engine limits even when the original prompt is tiny.
example: A hybrid-retrieval flag enables several rewrites while a large entitlement filter expands into many Boolean terms. The final serialized search request exceeds the engine's complexity ceiling and is rejected before ranking.
fooled: raising engine limits without bounding planning
logging the question but not the generated search request
prevent: Enforce a query-complexity budget before dispatch.
Cap rewrites, synonym expansion, filter cardinality and Boolean clauses.
Prefer set/lookup filters over giant OR lists where supported.
Provide a simpler retrieval fallback when the plan exceeds budget.
detect: Log clause count, rewrite count, filter cardinality and payload size.
Slice failures by feature flag, tenant and retrieval mode.
Alert before the hard engine limit, not only after rejection.
recover: Retry with a bounded fallback query, never the same oversized request.
Disable the expansion path via a safe feature switch.
Store the failed query plan as a regression case.
invariant: No generated retrieval plan reaches the search engine without passing a bounded complexity check.
closing: RAG can fail before retrieval. Observe the query you send, not just the question you received.
first_five: Capture the final serialized search plan and clause/filter counts.
Identify which rewrite/filter stage multiplied complexity.
Disable or bypass that stage and retry through a bounded fallback.
flow_caption: The input is small. The generated plan is not.

title: The LLM was fast. The AI request was waiting on SQL.
summary: Model telemetry can stay green while locks, plans, pools or queues dominate the user's end-to-end latency.
symptoms: Model latency is normal while total request latency climbs.
Several AI features slow down together.
Fixing a DB lock/plan/pool restores performance without changing the model.
failure_boundary: The user sees one AI request, but the critical path crosses ordinary distributed-system dependencies before and after inference.
why: AI observability often over-focuses on tokens and provider latency. That makes teams miss classic bottlenecks such as lock contention, connection-pool saturation, bad query plans, queue wait or a slow downstream API.
example: An agent reads prompt/config metadata before every model call. A blocking DB session holds a hot table. Inference itself is fast, but most user time is spent waiting before the model is even invoked.
fooled: service averages instead of critical-path spans
restarting AI workers for a shared DB bottleneck
prevent: Instrument separate spans for queue, DB, retrieval, model and tools.
Set dependency-specific timeouts/bulkheads and bounded pools.
Protect latency-sensitive paths from heavy administrative workloads.
Track and review query-plan/index changes on critical metadata paths.
detect: Compare model time with total request time.
Monitor lock waits, pool saturation and queue wait inside AI traces.
Alert on dependency contribution to latency, not only total latency.
recover: Remove blocking work or restore a known-good plan when appropriate.
Degrade non-critical reads if the product can do so safely.
Drain queued work gradually after recovery.
test: hold a lock on a hot path
change query plan while LLM remains healthy
invariant: Every AI latency regression can be decomposed into owned time across the full critical path.
closing: An AI system is still a distributed system; the model is not always what the user is waiting on.
first_five: Open one slow trace and account for every millisecond by span.
Inspect DB lock waits, pool saturation and plan changes before tuning the LLM.
Contain the blocking workload, then watch backlog drain rate.
flow_caption: The model is only one span on the critical path.

title: The safety check failed because its own dependency was down.
summary: Guardrails have availability dependencies too. The fail-open/fail-closed/degraded decision must be policy, not incident improvisation.
symptoms: Policy/guardrail calls fail because an upstream dependency is unavailable.
Low-risk reads and high-risk writes are blocked identically.
Operators consider bypassing the safety layer to restore service.
failure_boundary: The runtime cannot obtain a safety decision but must still decide what authority, if any, remains.
why: Safety services may depend on identity, policy stores, classification models or external APIs. If their outage mode is undefined, the product either stops unnecessarily or people create emergency bypasses under pressure.
example: A guardrail relies on an external identity/data service. That dependency fails. Read-only summarization and irreversible write actions now receive the same unavailable result even though their risk is very different.
fooled: testing jailbreaks but not guardrail infrastructure failure
prevent: Define outage policy by action risk: read, propose, reversible write, irreversible write.
Keep hard authorization enforcement in the runtime.
Cache only safe policy with explicit version and expiry semantics.
Minimize correlated dependencies between agent execution and authorization.
detect: Separate deny-rate from unavailable-rate.
Trace the exact dependency that prevented the decision.
Alert on degraded mode, bypass and cached-policy use.
recover: Enter pre-defined degraded mode; do not improvise authority.
Revalidate deferred actions after recovery.
Automatically expire any emergency override and audit every use.
invariant: Loss of a safety dependency must never silently grant more authority than the healthy system would allow.
closing: The guardrail has a failure mode too. Design it before the incident.
first_five: Distinguish POLICY_DENIED from POLICY_UNAVAILABLE.
Apply the pre-defined risk mode for the requested action class.
Keep high-impact writes blocked unless an alternate authoritative control exists.
flow_caption: Unavailable policy is different from denied policy.

title: The upgrade was compatible—until the agent actually ran.
summary: Schema compatibility can stay green while a platform, library, security or tool-runtime change breaks the workflow's behavior.
symptoms: A tool fails only after a platform/dependency/security rollout.
Registration/schema validation succeeds but execution fails.
Only some hosts fail because their runtime fingerprint differs.
failure_boundary: Static compatibility validates interfaces. Behavioral compatibility asks whether the same workflow still reaches the same verified state.
why: Agent workflows sit on Python/JVM libraries, sandbox policy, tool allowlists, serializers, MCP/API contracts and model behavior. A change can preserve the nominal interface while altering import, permission, execution or final-state semantics.
example: A security rollout narrows allowed function types. Existing configuration still parses, but one previously valid tool cannot load. Elsewhere, only hosts with a particular runtime package patch fail the same spreadsheet workflow.
fooled: health endpoint instead of synthetic execution
prevent: Pin/version runtime dependencies, policy and tool contracts with the agent release.
Maintain a model/tool/runtime compatibility manifest.
Run state-verified workflow regressions before platform changes.
Canary hosts/pods with fast rollback and explicit hold points.
detect: Compare failure rate by host/runtime/policy version.
Run synthetic tool executions, not only registration/health checks.
Alert on import, deserialize, policy-denial and execution regressions after rollout.
recover: Rollback or migrate to a supported contract.
Recreate contaminated runtime only when state can be reconstructed safely.
Turn the failing workflow into a permanent regression test.
test: upgrade one dependency with agent code unchanged
old vs new runtime same workflow
invariant: A release is compatible only if previously supported workflows still reach the expected externally verified state.
closing: Software compatibility is necessary. Behavioral compatibility is the production guarantee.
first_five: Group failures by runtime/policy/dependency fingerprint.
Compare canary/control on the same workflow and external final state.
Rollback the changed layer first; preserve the failing case before fixing it.
